description: Unipolar vs bipolar depression, ICD diagnosis, and biological and psychological theories.
content_html:
Depression and Everyday Sadness

Everyone feels sad or low from time to time — following a bereavement, a disappointment or a difficult period at school or work. This is a normal emotional response. Clinical depression is different. It is a persistent, debilitating condition that significantly impairs how a person thinks, feels and functions. The distinction matters because clinical depression requires professional assessment and, often, treatment.

Unipolar and Bipolar Depression

The spec identifies two main forms of clinical depression. Unipolar depression involves persistent low mood in only one direction — downward. A person with unipolar depression experiences prolonged periods of sadness, loss of interest and reduced energy, but does not experience episodes of abnormally high or elevated mood.

Bipolar depression involves cycling between episodes of very low mood and episodes of mania — abnormally elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and sometimes impulsive or risky behaviour. The shifts between these extremes can be rapid or may develop over weeks.

Key Fact

Unipolar depression: persistently low mood only. Bipolar depression: alternating episodes of very low mood (depression) and very high mood (mania). The key difference is that bipolar includes the manic phase; unipolar does not.

Diagnosing Unipolar Depression

The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is the diagnostic framework used to classify and diagnose unipolar depression. Diagnosis is not based on a single symptom but on the number and severity of symptoms present over a given period. The key symptoms the spec identifies are listed below.

Low mood: a persistent feeling of sadness, emptiness or hopelessness that does not lift for most of the day, most days.

Reduced energy levels: feeling fatigued and lacking the motivation or physical energy to carry out normal tasks, even simple ones.

Changes in sleep patterns: this can mean difficulty falling asleep, waking in the night, or sleeping far more than usual. Both insomnia and hypersomnia are associated with depression.

Changes in appetite levels: this may involve eating significantly less or significantly more than usual, often leading to noticeable weight change.

Decrease in self-confidence: a persistent sense of worthlessness, self-criticism or feelings of being a burden to others.

A diagnosis of unipolar depression requires that these symptoms are present in sufficient number and severity and that they represent a change from the person’s usual functioning. The ICD criteria prevent a clinician from diagnosing depression based on a brief, understandable reaction to a life event.

Biological Theory: The Influence of Nature

The biological explanation of depression focuses on what is happening inside the body. It proposes that depression results from an imbalance of neurotransmitters in the brain. In particular, the neurotransmitter serotonin is thought to play a central role. Research has linked lower levels of serotonin activity in the brain with the symptoms of depression, including persistent low mood, disrupted sleep and reduced appetite.

This is a “nature” explanation because it locates the cause of depression in physical, biological processes. It supports a reductionist approach: it reduces the experience of depression to brain chemistry. Antidepressant medications that increase serotonin availability — particularly SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which work by blocking the reabsorption of serotonin after it crosses the synapse — are effective for many people. Their effectiveness is often cited as indirect evidence supporting the serotonin theory: if raising serotonin activity reduces symptoms, this suggests low serotonin plays a role. However, the biological approach has limitations — not everyone with depression responds to SSRIs, which suggests brain chemistry alone cannot fully account for the condition.

The psychological explanation of depression focuses on the role of thought patterns and personal history — a “nurture” account. Aaron Beck (1979) proposed the cognitive triad: three interconnected patterns of negative thinking that maintain depression. These are a negative view of the self (“I am worthless”), a negative view of the world (“things always go wrong”), and a negative view of the future (“things will never improve”). These three perspectives reinforce each other and drive the depressive state. More broadly, the psychological approach proposes that depression arises from negative schemas and attributions. A schema is a mental framework for interpreting the world; a negative schema leads a person to interpret experiences in a consistently pessimistic and self-critical way, even when evidence for a more balanced view exists. These patterns tend to operate automatically — the person does not choose to think negatively, but finds their mind defaulting to worst-case interpretations.

Attributions are explanations a person gives for events. People who attribute failures to internal causes (“it is my fault”), stable causes (“this will always be true”) and global causes (“this affects everything in my life”) are more vulnerable to depression than those who make external, unstable and specific attributions (“that particular situation went wrong this time”). These negative thinking patterns can develop through early experiences of criticism, loss or failure, and once established they become self-reinforcing: a person in a low mood interprets new events negatively, which deepens the low mood further. The psychological approach is classified as a “nurture” explanation because it emphasises the role of experience and learning in shaping thinking styles.

Key Fact

Biological theory (nature): depression is caused by an imbalance of neurotransmitters, particularly low serotonin. Psychological theory (nurture): depression is caused by negative schemas and attributions — habitual patterns of pessimistic thinking developed through experience.
exam_tip_html: When describing the biological theory, always name the specific neurotransmitter (serotonin) and link it to the nature argument. When describing the psychological theory, use both terms — “negative schemas” and “negative attributions” — and explain what each means. On the 9-mark question, contrast these two theories as a nature–nurture debate and evaluate each: biological is reductionist but has treatment evidence; psychological is more holistic but harder to measure objectively.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Clinical depression differs from normal sadness by its persistence and severity. Unipolar depression involves only low mood; bipolar involves alternating low and high (manic) episodes.
  • Unipolar depression is diagnosed using the ICD framework, based on the number and severity of symptoms: low mood, reduced energy, changed sleep and appetite, and decreased self-confidence.
  • The biological theory attributes depression to a serotonin imbalance (nature); the psychological theory attributes it to negative schemas and attributions (nurture). Both offer partial, complementary explanations.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of depression involves alternating episodes of very low mood and mania?
A) Unipolar depression
B) Seasonal affective disorder
C) Bipolar depression
D) Reactive depression

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Definition states negative schemas are established patterns of negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future AND that they distort interpretation of experience — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one vague.
Developing: Mentions negative thoughts without reference to the schema framework or its distorting effect.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe three symptoms used to diagnose unipolar depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurately described symptom up to 3 marks. Students may include: low mood; reduced energy levels; changes in sleep patterns (insomnia or hypersomnia); changes in appetite (eating more or less); decrease in self-confidence/sense of worthlessness.
Mastering: Three distinct symptoms named and briefly described (what the symptom involves).
Secure: Three symptoms named with minimal description.
Developing: Two symptoms described.
Emerging: One symptom named or a vague reference to 'feeling sad'.

practice_questions.text: Explain the biological theory of depression, referring to the role of neurotransmitters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the neurotransmitter (serotonin), explains that low serotonin activity is linked to depression, identifies this as a nature explanation, and explains why (biological process, not experience), with development. Two developed points.
Secure: Serotonin named and linked to depression; nature explanation identified.
Developing: States that brain chemistry is involved but does not name serotonin or explain the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague reference to biology causing depression.

practice_questions.text: Describe the psychological theory of depression, including how negative schemas and attributions lead to low mood.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for: the theory is a nurture explanation (1); negative schemas are established negative thought patterns about self, world and future (1); these lead to pessimistic interpretation of experiences (1); negative attributions mean explaining failures as internal, stable and global causes (1); these patterns can develop through early experience and become self-sustaining (1).
Mastering: All five elements described with clear explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to thinking being negative, without schemas or attributions.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the biological and psychological theories of depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of both theories (serotonin imbalance for biological; negative schemas and attributions for psychological); identifies these as nature vs nurture explanations; at least two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. biological is reductionist but supported by effectiveness of SSRIs; psychological is more holistic but negative schemas are hard to measure objectively), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Both theories described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One theory described in detail; one evaluative point.
Emerging: One theory only or both described vaguely; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which neurotransmitter does the biological theory of depression particularly focus on?
Which framework is used to diagnose unipolar depression based on the number and severity of symptoms?
The psychological theory of depression focuses on _____ schemas and attributions as the cause of persistent low mood.
Unlike unipolar depression, _____ depression involves alternating episodes of very low mood and mania.
Match each symptom of unipolar depression to its description.
right: Persistent sadness or hopelessness most of the day
Fatigue and loss of motivation for normal tasks

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between unipolar and bipolar depression?
flashcard_questions.a: Bipolar includes manic (elevated mood) episodes; unipolar is low mood only.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the diagnostic framework used to classify unipolar depression.
Name five symptoms used to diagnose unipolar depression.
flashcard_questions.a: Low mood, reduced energy, changed sleep, changed appetite, decreased self-confidence.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the biological theory say causes depression?
flashcard_questions.a: An imbalance of neurotransmitters — particularly low serotonin activity in the brain.

flashcard_questions.q: What is serotonin's role in depression?
flashcard_questions.a: A neurotransmitter that regulates mood; lower levels are linked to depression.

flashcard_questions.q: Is the biological theory of depression a nature or nurture explanation?
flashcard_questions.a: Nature — it locates the cause in biological brain chemistry.

flashcard_questions.q: What are negative schemas in the psychological theory of depression?
flashcard_questions.a: Established patterns of negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future.

flashcard_questions.q: Is the psychological theory of depression a nature or nurture explanation?
flashcard_questions.a: Nurture — it locates the cause in thought patterns shaped by experience.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one strength of the biological theory of depression.
flashcard_questions.a: SSRIs increase serotonin and are effective for many patients — indirect evidence for the theory.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of the biological theory of depression.
flashcard_questions.a: It is reductionist — reducing a complex experience to brain chemistry alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What style of attribution makes a person most vulnerable to depression?
flashcard_questions.a: Attributing failures to internal causes — believing the fault lies within themselves.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do stable and global attributions increase depression risk?
flashcard_questions.a: Stable means the cause is seen as permanent; global means it affects all areas of life — creating a hopeless outlook.

glossary_terms.definition: A diagnosable medical condition characterised by persistent low mood and a range of cognitive, emotional and physical symptoms that go beyond normal sadness.
A form of depression characterised by persistently low mood without episodes of mania or elevated mood.
A form of depression characterised by alternating episodes of very low mood (depression) and abnormally high, elevated or irritable mood (mania).
The International Classification of Diseases — a global framework produced by the World Health Organisation used to classify and diagnose mental and physical health conditions.
A disruption in the levels of chemical messengers in the brain (neurotransmitters) that regulate mood and emotional processing.
A neurotransmitter that plays a key role in regulating mood, sleep, appetite and emotional wellbeing; lower levels are associated with depression.
The view that complex behaviours and mental states can be fully explained by reducing them to simpler biological or physical components.
Established patterns of negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future, which distort perception and maintain depression.
